chapter_theme: Through the cold and dewy seasons the women of Civakan's household drink, dress and revel; Gunamalai's sulk at the moon in her cup is ended by his flattery, and as spring comes the groves become a stage and the women adorn themselves for the spring sport.

cast.role: the hero, never named in this chapter's verses
Civakan's wife, who sulks at the moon in her cup
the women who dress and revel in the cold and spring seasons

2674.reading: The verse praises tender, doe-eyed women, said to be like does that have been startled; its middle lines are too obscure to construe with confidence.
2674.nuance: Lines 2 and 3 (யான றாமுலைப் பாலமுது, ஒன்றானும் மேவலர்) do not yield a certain sentence, so only the frame of praise is recorded.

2675.reading: When the cold season has come and moves about, the dark-lily-eyed women take to warm sandal paste for their full breasts, hot wine, opening-flower garlands, incense smoke and powder.
2675.nuance: The season is felt through what the women reach for: warmth and scent stand for the cold.
2675.event: The women, in the cold season, take to warming pastes, wine, garlands and incense.

2676.reading: Women in bee-humming garlands put out their beauty like buds, and the earth's king, thinking them sea-nectar, longs for them while the five arrows of spring's king press upon him.
2676.nuance: The one pressed by the arrows is called the earth's king (தரணி மன்னன்) without a name; the context makes Civakan likely, but the verse does not say so.

2677.reading: A woman tilts a cup of fire-coloured wine at her left side, sees the moon in it, and drinks it down as if to destroy a rival's shadow, then sulks as she looks at the sky.
2677.nuance: The sulk is aimed at the moon reflected in the wine, not at a person; who she is the verse does not say, though the next verse names Gunamalai.
2677.event: A woman sees the moon in her wine cup, drinks it and sulks.

2678.reading: Saying to the moon that she has drunk it and it hid and wasted with pallor yet lingers, Gunamalai sulks with eyes gone red, and he sets out to drive the sulk away by holding her close.
2678.nuance: The sulk is built on the moon-face conceit: she treats the reflected moon as a rival who has paled before her. The final line is left open and runs on into the next verse.
2678.event: Gunamalai sulks at the moon in her cup, and Civakan sets out to end the sulk by embracing her.

2679.reading: He tells her that the moon has darkened within and wasted in beauty before the light of her face, bids her not grieve in her heart, and takes her in his arms.
2679.nuance: The quarrel is ended by turning her own moon conceit into praise; he does not argue the sulk but flatters it away.
2679.event: Civakan consoles Gunamalai by saying the moon pales before her face, and embraces her.

2680.reading: As the dewy season that wilts the lotus arrives, the garlanded women wrap themselves in a cloak of fragrant rising smoke.
2680.nuance: The lotus's enemy is the cold season; the women answer it with smoke as a wrap.
2680.event: The women wrap themselves in incense smoke against the dewy season.

2681.reading: With smoke in their hair, sandal on their soft breasts, tamala garlands and serpent-like girdles, the women angrily scatter pearls.
2681.nuance: The scattering of pearls from a girdle is the poet's sign of lovers' passion or haste; the verse does not say who angers them.
2681.event: The women scatter pearls from their girdles.

2682.reading: The women, delighted, drink fruit wine and rice liquor and wear champak and jasmine garlands.
2682.event: The women drink fruit wine and rice liquor and put on champak and jasmine.

2683.reading: Garlands strike the women's eyes and their pearled breasts ache; anklets give a tired sound as hands are lifted, and desire sinks.
2683.nuance: The last clause, காமந் தாழ்ந்ததே, can be read as desire lowered or as passion grown heavy; the verse leaves it open.

2684.reading: The early dewy season passes entirely and the late dewy season comes to be tended, as the beauty of the women is dressed for it.
2684.nuance: The verse marks the turn of the cold seasons, early dew to late dew, and so places the chapter in the months leading to spring.

2685.reading: The women are described in white silk and white flower garlands, with red hips and jewelled ornaments gleaming like fire.

2686.reading: Kings give the women red blankets of fine fur warmed at the fire, which the women take gladly, and they are called peerless.
2686.nuance: The kings' gift is a cold-season comfort; the verse presents the women as receivers of royal gifts.
2686.event: Kings give the women fire-warmed red blankets, which they gladly take.

2687.reading: Daily the women live happily in the lower storey of a golden mansion that rubs the moon, delighting in dance and drinking the sound of song.
2687.event: The women pass their days in the golden mansion with dance and song.

2688.reading: In the lovers' battle between the curl-haired women and the heroes of the fine anklets, small drums, anklets, bells and girdles sound like the instruments of war.
2688.nuance: Lovemaking is figured as a battle, with the ornaments' sound as the war music.

2689.reading: The innocent women have bow-like brows and saffron on their breasts; bees settle on the paste in swarms, so that it seems laid down like brick, and it shines like the women's flower-hued bodies.
2689.nuance: The middle lines, வாய்ச்சியா லிட்டிகை செத்து, are hard to construe.

2690.reading: As the north wind goes and the southern breeze is sent as envoy, the trees bring out new leaves and flowers to welcome the coming of the spring king.
2690.nuance: The coming of spring is told as a guest's arrival: the breeze is the envoy and the trees prepare the welcome.
2690.event: The south breeze goes as envoy and the trees put out leaves and flowers to greet spring.

2691.reading: Bees are the lute, dark beetles the flute, cuckoos the drum and the scented groves the stage, and spring begins his feast-dance, taking as his call the loosened bangles and pallor of women whom lovers have left.
2691.nuance: The celebration is paid for by the parted women: their wasted wrists are what spring takes up as his song.
2691.event: Spring begins a feast-dance in the groves, with the bangles and pallor of forsaken women for his call.

2692.reading: Out of desire for spring sport the women grind nelli-fruit paste, rub civet-butter into their hair, bathe in scented water, perfume themselves with agil smoke, and put on fragrant powders.
2692.event: The women bathe, perfume and powder themselves for the spring sport.

2693.reading: The women gather jasmine garlands over their long plaits and set blue water-lilies in their ears.
2693.event: The women put jasmine garlands in their plaits and lilies in their ears.

2694.reading: The women put on smoke-coloured silk, golden girdles and ringing anklets, and adorn their calves and ankles.
2694.nuance: Line 3 has an odd spacing (சுமாஅய்க்கண்பின் பரூஉக்காம் பனைய கணைக் கால் சூழ்ந்) that makes the words hard to divide.

2695.reading: Thighs, golden makara ornaments and pearl strings on the breasts are described, with the pearls compared to a three-day crescent that gives off light like a rainbow.

2696.reading: The women's ears gleam with makara-shaped earrings and studs that outweigh their size in price.
2696.nuance: The gems are said to be small in size and very great in value.

2697.reading: Bright gem necklaces on the women's necks, large eyes feasting on darkness, pearl-bright teeth and coral lips like fruits all shine and bow.
2697.nuance: The last clause is hard to read; the pearl-and-coral figures are plain.

2698.reading: When evening has come and the women have dressed, they keep five-scent pastes in their cheeks and sit in the grove like flocks of peacocks, with anklets, bells and girdles sounding and their eyes like spear and blue lilies.
2698.event: The dressed women sit in the garden at evening.

links.note: The sulk of 2678 is answered by the consoling words and embrace of 2679.
links.teaches: The quarrel turns on one conceit: her sulk makes the moon a paled rival, and his answer keeps the moon and makes it pale before her face.

links.note: The husband tells his wife the moon pales before her face and thereby ends her sulk; Kural 1118 tells the moon it would be loved if it shone like her face.
links.teaches: The face-and-moon compliment is shown at work in a quarrel as a way to end a sulk, not only as praise.

gains.a: The conceit of the moon outshone by her face has a well-known formulation in a Kural couplet.
gains.b: A scene in which the same compliment is used to win a wife back from a sulk, which the couplet's address to the moon does not show.

links.note: The south breeze is sent as envoy to prepare the groves for spring; in the Silappathikaram's song the same breeze is the messenger who announces spring to the land.
links.teaches: The breeze as spring's herald serves different ends: the Cintamani uses it to dress the groves as a host's welcome, the Silappathikaram to bring the news to a Tamil land.

links.note: Spring's feast-dance in the groves rests on the loosened bangles of forsaken women; the Silappathikaram's closing venbas make spring the command that sulking lovers unite.
links.teaches: The same spring brings reunion for sulkers in one telling and shows the cost to women left apart in the other, so the season's joy is not shared by all.

source_issues: 2690-2698 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
2674 lines 2-3 and 2689 line 3 are hard to construe; 2694 line 3 has irregular word spacing; 2678 and 2685 end without a full stop.
